'''unharmed''' (un-härmd′), ''a.'' Not harmed or injured. ''Shak.'', R. and J., i. 1. 217.

'''unharmful''' (un-härm′fu̇l), ''a.'' Not harmful or doing harm; harmless; innoxious.
{{smaller block|Themselves ''unharmful'', let them live unharmed.
{{right|''Dryden'', Hind and Panther.}}}}

'''unharmfully''' (un-härm′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' Harmlessly; innoxiously. ''Contemporary Rev.'', LIV. 676.

'''unharmonious''' (un-här-mō′ni-us), ''a.'' Inharmonious.
{{smaller block|<poem>Those pure immortal elements that know
No gross, no ''unharmonious'' mixture.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xi. 51.}}}}

'''unharness''' (un-här′nes), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''harness.''] '''1.''' To strip of harness; loose from harness or gear; hence, to set free from work; release.
{{smaller block|An unmerciful day’s work of sorrow till death ''unharness'' them.
{{right|''Milton'', Divorce, ii. 21.}}
The sweating steers ''unharnessed'' from the yoke.
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Virgil’s Eclogues, ii. 96.}}}}
'''2.''' To remove armor or military dress from.

'''unhasp''' (un-hȧsp′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''unhaspen''; < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''hasp.''] To loose from a hasp; let go.
{{smaller block|<poem>While bolt and chain he backward roll’d,
And made the bar ''unhasp'' its hold.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., vi. 12.}}}}

'''unhasty''' (un-hās′ti), ''a.'' Not hasty; not precipitate; not rash; deliberate; slow.

'''unhazarded''' (un-haz′är-ded), ''a.'' Not exposed or submitted to hazard, chance, or danger; not ventured. ''Milton'', S. A., l. 809.

'''unhazardous''' (un-haz′är-dus), ''a.'' Not hazardous; not full of risk or danger; free from risk or danger. ''Dryden'', Duke of Guise, Epis.

'''unhead''' (un-hed′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''head.''] To take the head from; remove the head of; deprive of the head or of a head.
{{smaller block|You . . . did not only dare to uncrown, but to ''unhead'' a monarch. {{right|''T. Brown'', Works, ii. 216. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unheal<sup>1</sup>†''' (un-hēl′), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unheele'', ''unhele'', < AS. ''unhǣlu'', infirmity; as ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''heal''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''] Miserable condition; misfortune; wretchedness.
{{smaller block|<poem>Envy allone
That sory is of oother mennes wele,
And glad is of his sorwe and his ''unheele.''</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Physician’s Tale, l. 115.}}}}

'''unheal<sup>2</sup>†''' (un-hēl′), ''v. t.'' [Early mod. E. ''unhele'', ''unheel''; < ME. ''unheelen'', ''unhelen'', < AS. ''unhelan'', uncover; as ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''heal''<sup>2</sup>.] To uncover.
{{smaller block|<poem>Yit wol this werk the roote, as sum men telle,
''Unhele'', or kirve, and colde it after quelle.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 46.}}
<poem>Then suddeinly both would themselves ''unhele'',
And th’ amorous sweet spoiles to greedy eyes revele.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. xii. 64.}}}}

'''unheaven''' (un-hev′n), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''heaven.''] To remove from or deprive of heaven. [Rare.]

'''unheavenly''' (un-hev′n-li), ''a.'' Not heavenly; not pertaining to, characteristic of, or suitable for heaven. ''Byron'', Manfred, iii. 1. [Rare.]

'''unhedged''' (un-hejd′), ''a.'' Not hedged.
{{smaller block|<poem>Our needful knowledge, like our needful food,
''Unhedged'', lies open in life’s common field.</poem>
{{right|''Young'', Night Thoughts, v.}}}}

'''unheeded''' (un-hē′ded), ''a.'' Not heeded; disregarded; neglected; unnoticed.
{{smaller block|The world’s great victor passed ''unheeded'' by. {{right|''Pope.''}}}}

'''unheededly''' (un-hē′ded-li), ''adv.'' Without being noticed. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Beneath the fray
An earthquake reeled ''unheededly'' away.</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Childe Harold, iv.}}}}

'''unheedful''' (un-hēd′fůl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not heedful; heedless; not cautious; inattentive; careless. ''Tennyson'', The Gardener’s Daughter.—'''2.''' Not marked by caution or consideration; rash; inconsiderate.
{{smaller block|''Unheedful'' vows may heedfully be broken.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., ii. 6. 11.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|unhang|6613|unheeding}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''unhang''' (un-hang′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''unhung'' or ''unhanged'', ppr. ''unhanging''. [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''hang''.] '''1.''' To take or remove from a hanging position, as a picture or a bell, or a rapier from its hangers; also, to remove from its hinges or similar supports, as a door, a gate, or a shutter.
{{smaller block|Lend me thy boy to ''unhang'' my rapier.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Case is Altered, v. 2.}}}}
'''2.''' To deprive of hangings, as a room.

'''unhanged''' (un-hangd′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unhanged'', ''onhanged''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''hanged''.] Not hanged; not punished by hanging. Also ''unhung''.
{{smaller block|Thou ''on-hanged'' harlott, hark what I saie.
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 313.}}
There live not three good men ''unhanged'' in England.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., ii. 4. 144.}}}}

'''unhap†''' (un-hap′), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unhappe'', ''unhap'', ''onhap'', ''unhep'' (= Icel. ''ūhapp''); < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''hap''<sup>1</sup>.] Ill luck; misfortune.
{{smaller block|<poem>Sadly the segge hym in his sadel sette,
As non ''vnhap'' had hym ayled.</poem>
{{right|''Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 438.}}
Now certes, frend, I drede of thyn ''unhappe''.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Envoy to Scogan, l. 29.}}}}

'''unhappily''' (un-hap′i-li), ''adv.'' '''1.''' In an unhappy manner; unfortunately; miserably; evilly: as, to live ''unhappily''.
{{smaller block|<poem>Lucrece the chaste.
Haply that name of “chaste” ''unhappily'' set
This bateless edge on his keen appetite.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 8.}}
''Unhappily'' deceived. {{right|''Milton.''}}}} '''2.''' By ill fortune; as ill luck would have it; to some one’s misfortune: as, ''unhappily'' I missed seeing him.
{{smaller block|The commonplace is ''unhappily'' within reach of us all.
{{right|''Lowell'', New Princeton Rev., I. 177.}}}}
'''3.''' Not suitably or appropriately; not aptly.—'''4†.''' Trickishly; mischievously. ''Nares.''

'''unhappiness''' (un-hap′i-nes), ''n.'' '''1.''' The state or character of being unhappy, in any sense.—'''2.''' Misfortune; ill luck.
{{smaller block|It is our great ''unhappiness'', when any calamities fall upon us, that we are uneasy and dissatisfied. ''Abp. Wake.''}}
'''3†.''' A mischievous prank; wildness.
{{smaller block|<poem>I am Don Sanchio’s steward’s son, a wild boy,
That for the fruits of his ''unhappiness''
Is fain to seek the wars.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher and another'', Love’s Pilgrimage, ii. 2.}}}}

'''unhappy''' (un-hap′i), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unhappy'', ''unhappi'', ''onhappy''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''happy''.] '''1.''' Not happy. (''a'') Not cheerful or gay; in some degree miserable or wretched; cast down; sad.
{{smaller block|<poem>Ay me, ''unhappy!''
To be a queen! ''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iii. 2. 70.</poem>
<poem>''Unhappy'' consort of a king distrest!
Partake the troubles of thy husband’s breast.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xxiv. 234.}}}}
(''b'') Marked by or associated with ill fortune, infelicity, or mishap; inauspicious; ill-omened; calamitous; evil; lamentable.
{{smaller block|<poem>“I must,” quod he, “telle yow myn avise and entent;
The quene is cause of this ''onhappy'' case.”</poem>
{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 982.}}
<poem>''Unhappy'' was the clock
That struck the hour. ''Shak.'', Cymbeline, v. 5. 153.</poem>}}

{{smaller block|<poem>My dreams are like my thoughts, honest and innocent;
Yours are ''unhappy.''</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher and Rowley'', Maid in the Mill, i. 1.}}
Nothing indeed can be more ''unhappy'' than the condition of bankruptcy. {{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 456.}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'') Not felicitous; not well suited or appropriate; not apt.}} —'''2.''' Not having good hap, fortune, or luck; unfortunate; unlucky.
{{smaller block|I am a little ''unhappy'' in the mould of my face, which is not quite so long as it is broad. {{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 17.}}}}
'''3†.''' Full of tricks; mischievous; tricksy.
{{smaller block|''Laf.'' A shrewd knave, and an ''unhappy.''
''Count.'' So he is. My lord that ’s gone made himself much sport out of him. {{right|''Shak.'', All’s Well, iv. 5. 66.}}
<poem>Ay, and beat him well; he ’s an ''unhappy'' boy.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Burning Pestle, ii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn. 1.''' Downcast, cheerless.}}

'''unhappy†''' (un-hap′i), ''v. t.'' To make unhappy. ''Shak.'', Rich. II., iii. 1. 10.

'''unharbor, unharbour''' (un-här′bo̤r), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''harbor''<sup>1</sup>.] To drive from harbor or shelter; dislodge: a hunters’ word. ''Foote'', Devil upon Two Sticks, i.

'''unharbored, unharboured''' (un-här′bo̤rd), ''a.'' Not sheltered; affording no shelter. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Trace huge forests and ''unharbour’d'' heaths.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 423.}}}}

'''unhardened''' (un-här′dnd), ''a.'' Not hardened; not indurated: literally or figuratively.
{{smaller block|<poem>Messengers
Of strong prevailment in ''unharden’d'' youth.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., i. 1. 35.}}}}

'''unhardy''' (un-här′di), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unhardy'', ''unhardi''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''hardy''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' Not hardy; not able to endure fatigue or adverse conditions; tender.—'''2.''' Not having fortitude; not bold; timorous.
{{smaller block|Irresolute, ''unhardy'', unadventurous.
{{right|''Milton'', P. R., iii. 243.}}}}

'''unharmed''' (un-härmd′), ''a.'' Not harmed or injured. ''Shak.'', R. and J., i. 1. 217.

'''unharmful''' (un-härm′fu̇l), ''a.'' Not harmful or doing harm; harmless; innoxious.
{{smaller block|Themselves ''unharmful'', let them live unharmed.
{{right|''Dryden'', Hind and Panther.}}}}

'''unharmfully''' (un-härm′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' Harmlessly; innoxiously. ''Contemporary Rev.'', LIV. 676.

'''unharmonious''' (un-här-mō′ni-us), ''a.'' Inharmonious.
{{smaller block|<poem>Those pure immortal elements that know
No gross, no ''unharmonious'' mixture.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xi. 51.}}}}

'''unharness''' (un-här′nes), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''harness.''] '''1.''' To strip of harness; loose from harness or gear; hence, to set free from work; release.
{{smaller block|An unmerciful day’s work of sorrow till death ''unharness'' them.
{{right|''Milton'', Divorce, ii. 21.}}
The sweating steers ''unharnessed'' from the yoke.
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Virgil’s Eclogues, ii. 96.}}}}
'''2.''' To remove armor or military dress from.

'''unhasp''' (un-hȧsp′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''unhaspen''; < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''hasp.''] To loose from a hasp; let go.
{{smaller block|<poem>While bolt and chain he backward roll’d,
And made the bar ''unhasp'' its hold.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., vi. 12.}}}}

'''unhasty''' (un-hās′ti), ''a.'' Not hasty; not precipitate; not rash; deliberate; slow. {{smaller block|From her ''unhastie'' beast she did alight.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. iii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|He is a perfect man . . . who hath . . . so ''unhasty'' and wary a spirit as that he decrees upon no act before he hath considered maturely.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), I. 843.}}}}

'''unhat''' (un-hat′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''unhatted'', ppr. ''unhatting''. [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''hat''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To remove the hat from.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To take off the hat; uncover the head, as from politeness, or in worship.
{{smaller block|''Unhatting'' on the knees when the host is carried by.
{{right|''H. Spencer.''}}}}

'''unhatched<sup>1</sup>''' (un-hacht′), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''hatch''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' Not hatched; not having left the egg.—'''2.''' Not matured and brought to light; not disclosed.
{{smaller block|Some ''unhatched'' practice. {{right|''Shak.'', Othello, iii. 4. 141.}}}}

'''unhatched<sup>2</sup>†''' (un-hacht′), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''hatch''<sup>3</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>; or perhaps for ''unhacked'', not hacked.] Not hatched or marked with cuts or lines; not scratched or injured: applied in the quotations to a rapier not yet used in fight, both literally and figuratively.
{{smaller block|He is knight, dubb’d with ''unhatched'' rapier and on carpet consideration. {{right|''Shak.'', T. N., iii. 4. 257.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Tender and full of fears our blushing sex is,
Unharden’d with relentless thoughts, ''unhatch’d''
With blood and bloody practice.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Malta, ii. 5.}}}}

'''unhatting''' (un-hat′ing), ''n.'' A taking off of the hat, especially as an act of politeness, as in making a bow. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Bows, and curtseys, and ''unhattings.'' {{right|''H. Spencer.''}}}}

'''unhaunted''' (un-hän′ted), ''a.'' Not haunted; not frequented; not resorted to; unvisited.
{{smaller block|A lone ''unhaunted'' place. {{right|''Donne'', Prog. of the Soul, i.}}}}

'''unhazarded''' (un-haz′är-ded), ''a.'' Not exposed or submitted to hazard, chance, or danger; not ventured. ''Milton'', S. A., l. 809.

'''unhazardous''' (un-haz′är-dus), ''a.'' Not hazardous; not full of risk or danger; free from risk or danger. ''Dryden'', Duke of Guise, Epis.

'''unhead''' (un-hed′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''head.''] To take the head from; remove the head of; deprive of the head or of a head.
{{smaller block|You . . . did not only dare to uncrown, but to ''unhead'' a monarch. {{right|''T. Brown'', Works, ii. 216. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unheal<sup>1</sup>†''' (un-hēl′), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unheele'', ''unhele'', < AS. ''unhǣlu'', infirmity; as ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''heal''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''] Miserable condition; misfortune; wretchedness.
{{smaller block|<poem>Envy allone
That sory is of oother mennes wele,
And glad is of his sorwe and his ''unheele.''</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Physician’s Tale, l. 115.}}}}

'''unheal<sup>2</sup>†''' (un-hēl′), ''v. t.'' [Early mod. E. ''unhele'', ''unheel''; < ME. ''unheelen'', ''unhelen'', < AS. ''unhelan'', uncover; as ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''heal''<sup>2</sup>.] To uncover.
{{smaller block|<poem>Yit wol this werk the roote, as sum men telle,
''Unhele'', or kirve, and colde it after quelle.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 46.}}
<poem>Then suddeinly both would themselves ''unhele'',
And th’ amorous sweet spoiles to greedy eyes revele.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. xii. 64.}}}}

'''unhealable''' (un-hē′la̤-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being healed; incurable.
{{smaller block|An ''unhealable'' sprain.
{{right|''Fuller.''}}}}

'''unhealth''' (un-helth′), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unhelthe''; < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''health.''] Want of health; unhealthiness.
{{smaller block|Tens of thousands . . . lead sedentary and unwholesome lives . . . in dwellings, workshops, what not?—the influences, the very atmosphere of which tend not to health, but to ''unhealth'', and to drunkenness as a solace under the feeling of ''unhealth'' and depression.
{{right|''Kingsley'', Health and Education, p. 6.}}}}

'''unhealthful''' (un-helth′fu̇l), ''a.'' Not healthful; injurious to health; insalubrious; unwholesome; noxious, physically or morally: as, an ''unhealthful'' climate or air. ''Dryden'', tr. of Juvenal’s Satires, iv.

'''unhealthfully''' (un-helth′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' In an unhealthful manner; unhealthily.

'''unhealthfulness''' (un-helth′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unhealthful; unwholesomeness; insalubriousness. ''Bacon.''

'''unhealthily''' (un-hel′thi-li), ''adv.'' In an unwholesome or unsound manner. ''Milton'', Divorce, Pref.

'''unhealthiness''' (un-hel′thi-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unhealthy, in any sense.

'''unhealthy''' (un-hel′thi), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not healthy; lacking health; without vigor of growth; unsound: as, an ''unhealthy'' child; an ''unhealthy'' plant.—'''2.''' Not promoting health; unhealthful; unwholesome: as, ''unhealthy'' habits or food.—'''3.''' Not indicating health; resulting from bad health; morbid: as, an ''unhealthy'' sign or craving; an ''unhealthy'' appearance.—'''4.''' Morally unhealthful: as, ''unhealthy'' literature.

'''unheard''' (un-hėrd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not heard; not perceived by the ear.
{{smaller block|Heard melodies are sweet, but those ''unheard''
Are sweeter. {{right|''Keats'', Ode on a Grecian Urn.}}}}
'''2.''' Not admitted to audience or given a hearing; not permitted to speak for one’s self.
{{smaller block|What pangs I feel unpitied and ''unheard.'' {{right|''Dryden.''}}
Yet it was thought unjust to condemn him [Russell] ''unheard.'' {{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., xix.}}}}
'''3.''' Not known to fame; not celebrated.
{{smaller block|Nor was his name ''unheard.'' {{right|''Milton'', P. L., i. 738.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Unheard-of''', unprecedented; such as was never known or heard of before.}}
{{smaller block|We deeming it proper to apply some speedy Remedy to so enormous and ''unheard-of'' piece of Villany.
{{right|''Milton'', Letters of State, March 28, 1650.}}}}

'''unhearse†''' (un-hėrs′), ''v. t.'' [Early mod. E. ''unhearse''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''hearse''<sup>1</sup>.] To remove from a hearse or monument.
{{smaller block|And himselfe baffuld, and his armes ''unherst.''
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., V. iii. 37.}}}}

'''unheart†''' (un-härt′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''heart.''] To discourage; depress; dishearten.
<poem>Yet, to bite his lip
And hum at good Cominius much ''unhearts'' me.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., v. 1. 49.}}}}

'''unheaven''' (un-hev′n), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''heaven.''] To remove from or deprive of heaven. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|''Unheav’n'' yourselves, ye holy Cherubins.
{{right|''Davies'', Holy Roode, p. 28.}}}}

'''unheavenly''' (un-hev′n-li), ''a.'' Not heavenly; not pertaining to, characteristic of, or suitable for heaven. ''Byron'', Manfred, iii. 1. [Rare.]

'''unhedged''' (un-hejd′), ''a.'' Not hedged.
{{smaller block|<poem>Our needful knowledge, like our needful food,
''Unhedged'', lies open in life’s common field.</poem>
{{right|''Young'', Night Thoughts, v.}}}}

'''unheeded''' (un-hē′ded), ''a.'' Not heeded; disregarded; neglected; unnoticed.
{{smaller block|The world’s great victor passed ''unheeded'' by. {{right|''Pope.''}}}}

'''unheededly''' (un-hē′ded-li), ''adv.'' Without being noticed. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Beneath the fray
An earthquake reeled ''unheededly'' away.</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Childe Harold, iv.}}}}

'''unheedful''' (un-hēd′fůl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not heedful; heedless; not cautious; inattentive; careless. ''Tennyson'', The Gardener’s Daughter.—'''2.''' Not marked by caution or consideration; rash; inconsiderate.
{{smaller block|''Unheedful'' vows may heedfully be broken.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., ii. 6. 11.}}}}

'''unheedfully''' (un-hēd′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' Carelessly; incautiously. ''Shak.'', T. G. of V., i. 2. 3.

'''unheedily†''' (un-hē′di-li), ''adv.'' In an unheeding manner; carelessly; unheedingly. ''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. x. 13.
